title: Nucleus
summary: The nucleus is the command center of a eukaryotic cell — a membrane-bound sphere that holds most of the cell's DNA and coordinates activity like growth, division, and protein building. Explore the double nuclear membrane, the pores that control what enters and leaves, and the dense nucleolus, then see how the nucleus directs everything a cell does.

compareCandidate.label: Nucleus in prokaryotes vs. eukaryotes
compareCandidate.description: Eukaryotic cells (animals, plants, fungi, protists) have a true membrane-bound nucleus holding their DNA. Prokaryotic cells like bacteria have no nucleus — their DNA floats freely in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid.

processes: Transport across the nuclear envelope through pores
Reading DNA as the control center for cell activity
plainLanguageExplanation: The nucleus is like the brain of the cell — a rounded sac near the middle that acts as the control center. It is wrapped in a double layer called the nuclear envelope, and that envelope is not completely sealed: it is full of tiny holes called nuclear pores that work like doors, letting messages and materials in and out. Inside sits the nucleoplasm, and floating within it is the denser, darker nucleolus, plus most of the cell's DNA. The DNA holds all the instructions the cell needs, so the nucleus's job is to protect that instruction book and to decide which instructions get used. It decides it by 'reading' the DNA and sending copies of the needed instructions out through the pores to other parts of the cell, where they get turned into proteins. Because it controls every instruction, the nucleus coordinates division, growth, and nearly every activity the cell performs.

keyFacts.label: Where it sits
keyFacts.value: A large, usually central organelle found in all eukaryotic cells

keyFacts.label: Main job
keyFacts.value: Control center — stores and protects the cell's DNA and directs cell activity

keyFacts.label: Envelope
keyFacts.value: A double membrane that wraps the nucleus and separates it from the cytoplasm

keyFacts.label: Pores
keyFacts.value: Nuclear pores are openings in the envelope that control what enters and leaves, like a entrance gate

keyFacts.label: Nucleolus
keyFacts.value: A dense structure inside the nucleus where the cell builds the machine parts used by ribosomes

keyFacts.label: Found in
keyFacts.value: Eukaryotic cells only — bacteria and other prokaryotes keep their DNA loose in the nucleoid instead

whyItMatters: Almost every cell in your body has a nucleus running the show, so understanding it is the key to understanding how a single microscopic drop of protoplasm can carry the full plans for an entire organism. It's also the doorstep for genetics: the instructions in the DNA inside the nucleus are what make you you, and processes like DNA replication and transcription all begin here. When you learn about the nucleus, you unlock the whole story of how cells work, divide, and follow their instructions.
tagline: The command center of the cell
didYouKnow: A single human cell's nucleus holds about two meters of DNA packed tightly inside, yet that strand is thin enough to be invisible to the eye.
